claims.text: Conventionally powder-metallurgy-processed boride components have a relatively coarse grain structure.
Adding a rapid cooling step immediately after consolidation promotes refinement of the boride grains.
Rapid cooling produces narrower vulnerable grain-boundary regions.
Refinement of the boride microstructure reduces diffusion pathways available for molten-aluminum penetration.
Reduced percolation pathways limit intergranular corrosion by molten aluminum.
Limiting intergranular corrosion reduces degradation of the boride component.
Rapidly cooled components will have significantly lower molten-aluminum corrosion depths than conventionally processed, slower-cooled components under equivalent conditions.
Rapidly cooled components will have lower weight loss during molten-aluminum exposure than conventionally processed, slower-cooled components.
Rapidly cooled components will have longer service lifetimes than conventionally processed, slower-cooled components.
The corrosion-resistance improvement will persist at the elevated temperatures and under the dynamic molten-aluminum exposure typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
The predicted benefit depends on rapid cooling not introducing excessive residual stress or other unfavorable microstructural changes that compromise mechanical integrity.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-resistance improvement in the rapidly cooled group would falsify the hypothesis.
Mechanical harm that outweighs the corrosion benefit would falsify the hypothesis.
